soil-env-041.title: Phytostimulation: roots that feed pollutant-eating microbes
soil-env-041.text: Roots release carbohydrates and acids into the soil, and microbes respond. Phytostimulation, also called rhizodegradation, harnesses this to boost microbial breakdown of organic contaminants in the rhizosphere, the soil around roots. The stimulated microbes then biodegrade the contaminants. Plant litter and organic matter also help keep soil microbial diversity from being lost to contaminants. The approach has been tested with petroleum, PCBs and PAHs.

soil-env-042.title: Phytovolatilization: plants that release pollutants into the air
soil-env-042.text: Selenium can leave the soil through a plant as volatile dimethyl selenide, and mercury as the element. Phytovolatilization removes substances from soil or water through plants that turn them into more volatile, often less polluting forms and release them into the air. Poplars, with their high transpiration rates, have been promoted for removing volatile organic compounds.

soil-env-054.title: In situ thermal desorption: baking pollutants out of the ground
soil-env-054.text: Soil heated in place to as much as 900 °C gives up its pollutants by vaporization, steam distillation, oxidation or pyrolysis. In situ thermal desorption, also called thermal conduction heating, does exactly that, sometimes under vacuum. Arrays of electric or gas-fired thermal wells heat the soil by conduction, and vapor extraction wells collect the released contaminants. It works in tight soils such as clay, above and below the water table, at temperatures from under 100 °C to above the boiling point of water. Shell Oil developed it in the late 1980s from research on enhanced oil recovery, and commercialized it in the mid-1990s.

soil-env-022.title: Tracing a river's nutrient load back to its sources
soil-env-022.text: In Europe, agriculture is typically the main source of nitrogen in water bodies, while in many countries households and industry supply most of the phosphorus. Nutrient source apportionment estimates such shares: how much of the load reaching a water body comes from each sector, after attenuation or treatment. Load-oriented models work back from in-stream monitoring data. Source-oriented models calculate diffuse emissions from export coefficients of similar catchments. Ireland's Source Load Apportionment Model needs no in-stream data. It combines point discharges, diffuse land-use sources and catchment hydrogeology.

soil-env-021.title: Nutrient trading: a market for cleaner water
soil-env-021.text: Two polluters in the same watershed can face very different costs to control the same pollutant. Nutrient trading turns that gap into a market. It is a form of water quality trading in which polluters exchange credits for reducing nutrient pollution. Those with cheap controls sell reduction credits to those with costly ones. Its principle is 'polluter pays', usually tied to a regulatory requirement to take part. A 2013 review found three kinds of funders: beneficiaries, polluters and public good payers. Governments and NGOs initiated most payments.

soil-env-204.title: Point source pollution: one pipe, one smokestack
soil-env-204.text: A single factory outfall or smokestack is the classic point source. Point source pollution comes from one identifiable source, so small in extent that models can treat it as a mathematical point. That sets it apart from nonpoint and area sources. Water point sources include factories, power plants, municipal sewage treatment plants and some farms, such as concentrated animal feeding operations. They can contaminate natural, man-made and groundwater reservoirs, threatening human health.

soil-env-056.title: Surfactant leaching: flushing oily contaminants from soil
soil-env-056.text: Surfactants are compounds that let oil and water blend, and they can wash pollution out of the ground. Surfactant leaching mixes contaminated water or soil with surfactants, then leaches out the emulsified contaminants. In surfactant-enhanced aquifer remediation, surfactant solution is pumped from injection wells through contaminated zones to extraction wells. It removes non-aqueous phase liquids, pollutants that stay separate from water. In oil recovery the commonest surfactants are ethoxylated alcohols and nonylphenols, sulfates, sulfonates and biosurfactants.

soil-env-203.title: Radioactive contamination: fallout in the soil
soil-env-203.text: Between the 1950s and 1980s, 520 atmospheric nuclear explosions spread fallout widely. Radioactive contamination is the unintended presence of radioactive substances on surfaces or within solids, liquids or gases. It is hazardous because their decay emits ionizing radiation. Some sources are natural. Uranium, thorium and their decay products occur in rock and soil, and mining, oil and gas extraction and coal use can concentrate them. Others are man-made. A nuclear weapon blast or reactor breach contaminates nearby air, soil, people, plants and animals with fuel and fission products, as around Chernobyl and Fukushima. The hazard depends on the concentration, the energy and type of radiation, and how close the contaminants come to body organs. Large contaminated areas may be covered with concrete, soil or rock to stop spread, and cleanup itself produces radioactive waste. After Fukushima, one goal was to strip 80 to 95% of cesium-137 from soil without destroying its organic content. The aim was to bring exposure down to 1 mSv a year above background.

soil-env-034.title: Fungi that soak up metals, and even gold
soil-env-034.text: Filtering electronic waste through fungi has recovered 80% of its gold. Fungal biosorption is the capture of metals by fungi, which bind them on their cell surfaces and concentrate them in their fruiting bodies for later removal. Pleurotus, Aspergillus and Trichoderma remove lead, cadmium, nickel, chromium, mercury, arsenic, copper and zinc, on land and in water. Metals enter the mycelium passively, and strains from long-polluted sites tolerate them best. Some mushrooms become bioindicators: the edible shaggy ink cap signals mercury well, but can then be toxic to eat. Even dead fungal cell walls can filter heavy metals and radionuclides from industrial effluents.

soil-env-035.title: Fungi that digest pollutants the way they digest wood
soil-env-035.text: Lignin and cellulose are long-chain carbon compounds, much like many organic pollutants. That resemblance explains fungal degradation of organic pollutants. Fungi, especially {{ref:soil-bio-129}}, break pollutants down with the enzymes and acids they secrete to digest lignin and cellulose. The enzymes include lignin peroxidase, manganese peroxidase, laccase and cytochrome P450. Fungi degrade petroleum fuels, phenols, polyurethane and PCBs in soil, though sometimes they only prepare the way for later microbial activity. White rot fungi break down the pesticides endosulfan, chlorpyrifos and atrazine in clay-loam soils, and dyes such as the carcinogenic Congo red.

soil-env-036.title: Mycorrhizal fungi as partners in plant cleanup
soil-env-036.text: Fungal threads can stretch a plant's reach beyond its roots. Mycorrhizoremediation uses mycorrhizal fungi to remove soil contaminants and so strengthen phytoremediation. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi relieve plants' pollutant stress, so the plants grow more biomass, and they supply nutrients, especially phosphorus. The fungi also make proteins that bind heavy metals, lowering their bioavailability. Their fast-spreading mycelium extends the root zone into the hyphosphere, reaching more nutrients and contaminants and boosting helpful bacteria. Pairing Rhizophagus intraradices with Robinia trees or vetiver grass has removed lead, and mycorrhizal reeds have degraded benzene and MTBE from wetland groundwater.

soil-env-202.title: Permeable reactive barriers: a treatment wall for groundwater
soil-env-202.text: A permeable reactive barrier is a treatment zone set across a contaminant plume, cleaning groundwater as it flows through. It is built by digging a trench across the groundwater flow, filling it with reactive material such as iron, carbon or limestone, and covering it with soil. Contaminants are immobilized by sorption or precipitation, which may require replacing the medium. Or they are transformed into less harmful forms, usually by redox reactions. Zerovalent iron was the first barrier material and remains the main one. Barriers most likely fail by losing reactivity rather than permeability, and estimates of their life range from 10 to 100 years.

soil-env-049.title: DRASTIC: scoring how easily an aquifer is polluted
soil-env-049.text: Seven factors spell DRASTIC: depth to water, net recharge, aquifer media, soil media, topography, impact of the vadose zone and hydraulic conductivity. Together they make an index, often mapped with GIS, that rates how prone an aquifer is to contamination. Each factor carries a weight from one to five. A lower index means a lower risk of contamination. The score shows authorities which areas are most vulnerable, so they can put protective measures in place.

soil-env-052.title: Metallophytes: plants that live on metal-rich ground
soil-env-052.text: Some plants survive only where heavy metals are present. A metallophyte is a plant able to survive in metal-rich soil. Obligate metallophytes are confined to such soils, while facultative ones tolerate metals but are not restricted to them. They fall into three classes. Metal excluders absorb metals only at their roots. Metal indicators accumulate heavy metals in shoots and leaves but eventually succumb to their toxicity. The third class is described in {{ref:soil-env-050}}.

soil-env-050.title: Hyperaccumulators: plants that store metal in their leaves
soil-env-050.text: Alpine pennycress can hold up to 380 mg/kg of cadmium in its leaves. It is a hyperaccumulator, a metallophyte that absorbs metals through its roots and stores them in its leaves. Such plants concentrate metals to levels toxic to related species not adapted to metal-rich soils, and about 85–90% of them are obligate metallophytes. One threshold is over 1000 mg/kg of dry weight for nickel, copper, cobalt, chromium or lead, and over 10,000 mg/kg for zinc or manganese. About 450 species, including Arabidopsis and other Brassicaceae, take up metals at 100–1000 times the levels in sister species. Toxic leaves may deter herbivores and pathogens, the 'elemental defense hypothesis'. These plants are widely discussed for cleanup, but commercial use remains aspirational. After the Chernobyl accident, sunflowers removed cesium-137 and strontium-90 from a pond. Introduced species can also invade. Nickel-accumulating Alyssum, brought to Oregon in the 1990s to harvest metal, spread into serpentine habitats and was declared a noxious weed in 2009.

soil-env-051.title: Phytomining: farming metal from the soil
soil-env-051.text: In 1983 Rufus Chaney, a USDA agronomist, proposed harvesting metals with plants. Phytomining, also called agromining, extracts heavy metals with hyperaccumulating plants, then collects and refines the metals from the harvested biomass. Chaney and Alan Baker first tested it in 1996. In principle it could harm the environment less than conventional mining and recover low-grade metals from mine waste. Practice has lagged. A 2021 review judged its commercial viability limited because it is slow and inefficient. By mid-2024 one nickel project had extracted less than a kilo of usable nickel. Still, in 2025 a start-up raised 45 million dollars to commercialize nickel phytomining from mine tailings.

soil-env-046.title: Cleaning the vapor that soil extraction pulls out
soil-env-046.text: The gas drawn from a soil vapor extraction well is still contaminated. SVE off-gas treatment cleans it before release, most often by thermal oxidation or adsorption on activated carbon. The choice depends on the contaminant, its concentration, throughput and cost. Granular activated carbon suits streams below 500 ppmV, oxidation those up to 4,000 ppmV, and vapor condensation those above. Thermal oxidizers run at 730 to 820 °C, while catalytic oxidizers work at 316 to 427 °C. Activated carbon must be replaced as it saturates, and it does not remove heavy metals. Incineration is controversial because it risks releasing dioxins.

soil-env-032.title: Bioaugmentation: adding specialist microbes to a polluted site
soil-env-032.text: Municipal wastewater plants commonly add microbial cultures to restart their activated-sludge bioreactors. That is bioaugmentation, a type of bioremediation that adds specialized microbes to boost the breakdown of pollutants. Elsewhere it remains more aspirational than practical at scale. For soils it has been proposed against chlorocarbons from dry cleaners and hydrocarbons from gas stations, usually with biostimulation to favor dechlorinating microbes. Failures come from the wrong organism, predation, competition with native bacteria and too-small doses. Many trials weighed only a strain's degrading ability, not its fitness among the existing microbes.

soil-env-043.title: Rhizofiltration: roots that strain metals from water
soil-env-043.text: In one study, sunflower roots cut uranium levels by nearly 95% in 24 hours. Rhizofiltration is phytoremediation that filters contaminated groundwater, surface water or wastewater through a mass of roots to remove toxic substances or excess nutrients. Like phytoextraction, it traps contaminants, mainly heavy metals, in harvestable biomass, but it treats water rather than soil. Plants are usually raised in a greenhouse first, then planted at the site or fed contaminated water brought to them. Removing radionuclides with sunflowers was estimated at $2 to $6 per thousand gallons treated. It misses contaminants below rooting depth, can take years, and harvested plants threaten health unless non-fodder crops are used.

soil-env-013.title: Contaminated land risk assessment: how much is too much
soil-env-013.text: Nobody wants to pay for assessing or cleaning contaminated land, and findings on nearby plots may go on property titles and lower their value. That makes contaminated land risk assessment contentious. It is the staged evaluation of whether a site's contaminants pose unacceptable risk. It moves from a qualitative conceptual site model to generic and then detailed quantitative assessment. Work starts once a site is suspected of contamination, often with a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment, and the site's past uses guide sampling and analysis. Generic screening values are set conservatively for standard land uses. Exceeding one shows only that harm is possible, prompting site-specific study of contaminants, pathways and receptors. Neighboring land is often contaminated too, by decades of emissions or contaminated fill. So nearby topsoil, ceiling dust and water should be tested before and after remediation. National standards include the US EPA's Regional Screening Levels, the Dutch standards, Australia's investigation levels and Canada's provincial standards. The EU is moving towards Europe-wide standards, though most industrialized European nations still set their own.

reviews.contamination-and-remediation: Soil contamination starts at mines, factories, spills, farm fields and waste dumps, and it ends in people's food, water and dust. Some pollutants never break down: heavy metals cannot be degraded, while persistent organic pollutants such as DDT and PFAS travel to the poles and concentrate up food chains. Other harm is diffuse, as nitrogen and phosphorus leaving fields drive eutrophication and dead zones far downstream. Cleanup ranges from digging soil out and walling it in to drawing off vapors, heating the ground or passing electric current through it. Bacteria, fungi and plants offer cheaper, gentler cleanup, but they are slow, rarely used at scale, and can only lock up or harvest the metals they cannot destroy.
